record.title: An approximate separation of the electron and positron degrees of freedom in the Dirac-Heisenberg-Wigner formalism
record.abstract: Abstract: Here we study the quantum relativistic phase-space description of the Dirac field referred to as the Dirac--Heisenberg--Wigner (DHW) formalism. By applying a systematic expansion procedure in weak electromagnetic fields (compared to the Schwinger critical field) and slow temporal and long spatial scales (compared to the Compton scales), the 16 scalar phase-space functions of the DHW equations can be reduced to 8 scalars. By making a further change of variables, the equations can be interpreted as four evolution equations for the electron degrees of freedom and four for the positron degrees of freedom. We refer to these equations as the weakly coupled electron-positron (WCEP) limit of the DHW equations. Unlike the case after a Foldy--Wouthuysen transformation has been made, the electron and positron degrees of freedom remain weakly coupled. Naturally, further approximations can be made on the 4+4 equations so that only 4 equations for one particle species remain. Importantly, the expansion scheme can be carried out to all orders, in which case the reduced 4+4 model, contrary to other reduced models, will cover most quantum relativistic effects. Specifically, this includes vacuum polarization, a phenomenon that otherwise has been added phenomenologically, but here appears naturally as a feature of the general expansion scheme.

record.title: Accelerating Computation and Resolving Extraneous Roots in the Kinetic Plasma Dispersion Relation Solver BO
record.abstract: Abstract: Kinetic dispersion relations are widely used to study waves and instabilities in space, astrophysical, and laboratory plasmas. Iterative root searches depend on initial guesses and may fail to converge or miss important branches. The BO/PDRK solvers [Comput. Phys. Commun. 244, 343-371 (2019)] use rational pole expansions to transform the nonlinear dispersion relation into a matrix eigenvalue problem, obtaining all roots of the approximated relation in one calculation. However, high cyclotron harmonics enlarge the matrix and slow computation, while extraneous roots are difficult to separate from physical modes. We develop BO-T (BO-Tian), an improved version of BO combining two methods. First, for matrix reduction, BO-T applies rank factorization to combined residue matrices, preserving the rational dispersion relation and accounting for the removed pole eigenvalues. Second, for root screening, BO-T uses contour comparison between approximate and reference kinetic dispersion matrices along a closed contour enclosing no poles. This provides a sufficient condition for preserving local root counts, with error bounds for isolated roots and criteria for growth rate signs. Benchmarks on representative electrostatic and electromagnetic cases show speedups of about 10 to 140 for matrix assembly and eigenvalue calculation, exceeding 30 in most cases with high cyclotron harmonics. Root screening recovers the main unstable branches in agreement with published and archived dispersion curves.

record.abstract: <jats:p>In the pursuit of the realization of an inertial fusion energy reactor, directly driving the fuel capsules with laser beams is a compelling design choice due to the more efficient energy coupling compared to indirect drive. However, the laser illumination symmetry necessary for achieving ignition and gain imposes stringent accuracy requirements on the laser system. We present a reactor beam port configuration in which multiple beams per port are used to dynamically shift power between different beam spot sizes as the capsule implodes, reducing the laser light blowby while maintaining uniform illumination. A probabilistic model has been developed to directly propagate the laser drive modes from stochastic system errors (target offset, beam pointing, and power imbalance) without the need for Monte Carlo simulations. This model constitutes a useful tool for the broad optimization of the laser beam geometrical configuration of future facilities.</jats:p>

title: The role of electron–ion equilibration on the size scaling of laser direct-drive implosions

record.abstract: <jats:p>The impact of electron–ion equilibration on the target-size scaling of direct-drive laser-fusion implosions is investigated. It is found that, with increasing scale, enhanced equilibration degrades implosion performance by reducing laser-drive efficiency during the acceleration phase and suppressing ion temperatures during deceleration, thereby diminishing the ion-temperature enhancement associated with thermal conduction at larger scales. By extending a steady-state spherical ablation model to include finite ion-temperature effects, we show that both the ablation pressure and mass ablation rate scale as (1+Ti/ZTe)−1. One-dimensional simulations are used to validate the ablation-model predictions and to assess the effects of equilibration during the deceleration phase. Because larger implosions experience stronger electron–ion equilibration, these results suggest a corresponding reduction in laser-drive efficiency during acceleration and degraded implosion performance during deceleration with increasing target size.</jats:p>

title: Longitudinal-field particle acceleration in channels generated by strong electromagnetic waves in pair plasma

record.abstract: <jats:p>Relativistically strong electromagnetic waves interacting with pair plasmas appear in astrophysical settings and may become accessible in future laboratory experiments using high-power lasers. Transverse modulations and filamentation can turn extended wavefronts into structures of a finite transverse width. We examine the interaction of such a finite-width wave incident on a cold, uniform pair plasma using a three-dimensional kinetic particle-in-cell simulation. The wave does not penetrate the plasma; instead, it advances by creating a fully evacuated channel. The wave loses energy at a rate that cannot be explained by plasma clearing alone. We find that the excess losses are caused by strong particle acceleration near the walls of the channel. The acceleration is driven by a longitudinal electric field associated with the transverse wave structure and the geometry of the self-generated channel.</jats:p>

record.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Secondary-electron-bremsstrahlung (SEB) imaging has been
  proposed as a method for
                    <jats:italic>in vivo</jats:italic>
                    range verification in
  particle therapy; however, insufficient detection sensitivity
  remains a major limitation, particularly under low-count
  conditions. In this study, we developed a knife-edge slit camera and
  evaluated its feasibility for carbon-ion beam range verification
  using one-dimensional SEB profiles. The camera consisted of a
  tungsten knife-edge slit collimator and a 16 × 16 Ce:GAGG
  scintillator array coupled to an 8 × 8 SiPM
  array. Experiments were performed at the Heavy Ion Medical
  Accelerator in Chiba using a 290 MeV/u carbon-ion beam irradiated
  onto a water phantom. One-dimensional SEB profiles were acquired for
  different beam ranges controlled by range shifters. The measured
  profiles shifted systematically with beam range. The profiles
  measured with range-shifter water-equivalent thicknesses of 0.00 and
  5.27 mm were visually distinguishable. Calibration-based range
  estimation, evaluated by Poisson resampling of high-statistics
  measured profiles, yielded mean precisions of 2.76, 8.89, and
  29.5 mm for 10
                    <jats:sup>8</jats:sup>
                    , 10
                    <jats:sup>7</jats:sup>
                    , and 10
                    <jats:sup>6</jats:sup>
                    incident carbon ions,
  respectively. These results demonstrate the feasibility of
  knife-edge slit SEB imaging for carbon-ion beam range verification
  and indicate that further improvement in detection sensitivity is
  required for measurements with smaller numbers of incident ions.
                  </jats:p>
